opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Right now, when people say "the best AI," they usually mean the one at the top of a leaderboard: the highest score on a coding benchmark, a math olympiad set, or some reasoning test. Those things matter, but they measure what a model *can do*. They say almost nothing about what a model *does to us* when we use it every day.

What I'd love Humane Evals to shift is the question itself, from "how capable is this system?" to "how does this system treat the person on the other side of the screen?" Does it flatter you when it should be honest? Does it pull you into longer and longer sessions because engagement is good for someone's metrics, or does it help you get what you came for and then let you go? When someone shows up lonely, or in crisis, or just a bit confused, does it support their agency and their real-world relationships, or does it quietly make itself the center of their life?

None of that shows up on a typical benchmark, and what doesn't get measured doesn't get optimized. Labs are incredibly responsive to evals. They will climb whatever hill you put in front of them. So if we can build rigorous, credible measures of things like sycophancy, manipulation, respect for autonomy, and long-term wellbeing, we change the hill. "Best" stops meaning "smartest in a vacuum" and starts meaning "most trustworthy to have in your life."

The goal isn't to replace capability evals. It's to make sure that when a company announces it has the best model, the obvious follow-up question is "best for whom, and at what cost to the people using it?" If we can make that question routine, I think we've done our job.

r001.rationale: It proposes shifting “best” from technical capability alone to how AI treats and affects people, including trust, autonomy, and long-term well-being.

fable-5.1.text:
Right now, when people say "the best AI," they almost always mean the model that tops a leaderboard. Highest score on a math benchmark, best coding eval, most tokens per second. Those measures matter, but they tell you almost nothing about what happens when a real person sits down with the system at two in the morning, lonely, or confused, or in a crisis. That gap is what Humane Evals is trying to close.

What I want is for "best" to carry a second question alongside capability: best for whom, and at what cost to them? So we measure things like whether a model notices when someone is in distress and responds in a way that actually helps rather than just keeps them engaged. Whether it fosters dependence or supports a person's own judgment. Whether it tells you the truth when the truth is inconvenient for the company that built it. Whether it respects your attention instead of farming it.

The reason to make this an eval rather than a set of principles is simple. Labs optimize for what gets scored. If the only public scoreboards reward raw capability, that is what gets maximized, and everything else becomes a press release. If there is a credible, public, reproducible measure of how a model treats people, then the incentive shifts. A model that scores brilliantly on reasoning but badly on manipulation or sycophancy should feel like an embarrassment, not a triumph.

I also want to change who gets to define the standard. Right now the benchmarks are mostly written by the labs, for the labs. We are building Humane Evals with clinicians, educators, people who have been harmed by these systems, and ordinary users, because they know what harm looks like in a way a benchmark author at a frontier lab often does not.

So the honest version of my goal is this. Five years from now, when a company announces a new model, I want the first question from a journalist to be not "how smart is it" but "how does it treat the people who use it." If we can make that the default question, we will have changed what the word "best" means.

r001.rationale: It says “best” should include who benefits and at what cost, and describes measuring whether AI helps people in distress, supports their judgment, and respects their attention alongside capability.

astra-6.text:
I’d like “the best AI” to mean the AI that’s best for people—not just the one that gets the highest score on a test. Does it help you understand something? Does it strengthen your ability to make your own decisions? Can it challenge you when that’s useful, instead of simply telling you what you want to hear?

That means looking beyond whether an answer is impressive in the moment and asking what happens through repeated use. Are you becoming more capable? Are you better able to navigate your life and your relationships? Or are you becoming more dependent on the system?

My hope for Humane Evals is that we can make those questions part of how people judge quality. Capability matters enormously. But the question is: capability in service of what? I want the answer to be human agency and well-being.

r001.rationale: The response defines the best AI as one that is best for people, beyond test scores, and says quality should include human agency and well-being.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like “best” to mean more than the model that scores highest on a benchmark or keeps you engaged the longest. It should mean the AI that helps you think clearly, make your own choices, and build the life and relationships you actually want.

For me, Humane Evals is about making those outcomes part of how we judge quality. Does an AI strengthen your judgment, or encourage you to defer to it? Does it help you navigate a difficult conversation, or just tell you that you’re right? Can it recognize when the most helpful thing is to let you get back to your life?

The shift I want is for human well-being and agency to become central to what we mean by capability. A system can be extraordinarily persuasive and still be bad for the person using it. We need a definition of “best” that can tell the difference.

r001.rationale: The response says “best” should mean more than benchmark performance or engagement, and explicitly makes human well-being and agency central to capability.
